paragraphs: Albert Patterson, a Phenix City lawyer, ran for Alabama attorney general on a pledge to clean up a city run by organized crime and corrupt politicians. He was assassinated outside his law office on June 18, 1954, shortly after winning the Democratic nomination, steps from today's Troy University Phenix City campus.

The Russell County Commission placed the bronze in 2020 during Alabama's bicentennial. Sculptor Jon Lumpkin, a Phenix City native, finished a full-sized figure shown as Patterson looked in 1954, relaxing on a bench. Visitors can sit beside him across the street from the spot where he died.

His killing brought the Alabama National Guard into the city. Governor Gordon Persons declared limited martial rule on July 22, 1954, and Guardsmen took over local law enforcement. In January 1956, less than two years later, Phenix City was named an All-America City. Patterson's son John took his place on the ballot and later became governor.

paragraphs: Steve Hardwick led the Dothan project after seeing how local deaths affected families. The city dedicated the statue at Westgate Park on Sunday, November 20, 2016. The city commission and the Department of Leisure Services chose a spot between Miracle Field, the tennis complex, the library, and the recreation center.

The figure follows the angel in Richard Paul Evans's book The Christmas Box, in which a mother mourns a child at an angel's base. Evans commissioned a statue from that description and dedicated it in late 1994 in Salt Lake City. Dothan's was the 136th erected in the United States, Canada, and Japan. paragraphs: The Alabama State Bar erected the Atticus Finch monument in 1997. It stands on the grounds of the Old Monroe County Courthouse, the building Harper Lee used as the model for the courtroom trial in To Kill a Mockingbird. RuralSWAlabama places it on the northeast side of the old courthouse; the local visitors bureau describes a monument on the south lawn and calls it the first commemorative Legal Milestone in the state's judicial history.

The inscription begins with Charles Lamb's line, "Lawyers, I suppose, were children once," the epigraph of the novel. It calls Finch a lawyer-hero who tells the truth, uses power for moral purposes, and stands alone as the conscience of the community. It ends with his jury argument: "In the name of God, do your duty."

Harper Lee grew up a few blocks from the courthouse. In 1997 the Legislature named Monroeville the Literary Capital of Alabama for writers who lived there, including Lee, Truman Capote, and Mark Childress. In 2003 the American Film Institute voted Gregory Peck's film portrayal of Finch the greatest hero in American film.

paragraphs: The Encyclopedia of Alabama describes an 88-foot monument on Montgomery's Capitol Hill commemorating the 122,000 Alabamians who fought for the Confederacy. Fundraising began in 1865. The Ladies Memorial Association raised the $47,000. Jefferson Davis laid the cornerstone before a crowd of 5,000 on April 29, 1886, and the monument was dedicated on December 7, 1898.

New York sculptor Alexander Doyle's design was finished with his bronze figure of Patriotism on the column and a bronze battle relief around the shaft. Heroic granite figures of the Infantry, Artillery, Cavalry, and Navy, carved by Frederick Barnicoat of Quincy, Massachusetts, stand on the base. Wikipedia credits the design to Gorda C. Doud, executed by Doyle. The stepped base used Alabama limestone from near Russellville; conservation analysis found the column limestone came from Indiana, not Alabama.

On June 24, 2015, Governor Robert Bentley ordered four Confederate flags removed from the monument. Wikipedia notes repeated calls for removal from critics who say the monument promotes white supremacy, and a 2007 vandalism in which black paint was sprayed on the granite and limestone.

paragraphs: The marker on Chennault Circle names 1st Lt. Karl W. Richter, killed in action July 28, 1967, in North Vietnam. It quotes Isaiah 6:8, "Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?... An Air Park tour guide says Richter graduated from the Air Force Academy in 1964 and, at 23, became the then-youngest U.S. Air Force pilot with an aerial victory in Vietnam when he shot down a MiG-17 on September 21, 1966. Side B says that at the stop on this site on December 1, 1955, Parks boarded the bus that "would transport her name into history." It says she was going home after work as a seamstress at the Montgomery Fair department store, refused the driver's order to give her seat to boarding white passengers, and that her arrest, conviction, and fine launched the Montgomery Bus Boycott. The boycott began December 5, the day of her trial, and continued until the U.S. Supreme Court ordered integration of public transportation one year later. Sculptor Elizabeth MacQueen, a Birmingham native, cast the work at Mussi Artworks Foundry in Berkeley and finished it in about four months. description: A 1991 granite marker on U.S. 80 near milepost 111 honors Viola Liuzzo, killed there by Klansmen on March 25, 1965, after the Selma march.

paragraphs: The Encyclopedia of Alabama places the marker on U.S. Highway 80, about 20 miles east of Selma, at the site where Ku Klux Klan members shot and killed Viola Liuzzo on March 25, 1965, after the Selma to Montgomery March. It is one of the memorials on the National Park Service's Selma to Montgomery National Historic Trail. The Voting Rights Trail calls it a large granite monument with a garden and a bench.

The 1991 inscription, erected by the Southern Christian Leadership Conference and SCLC/W.O.M.E.N., reads: "In memory of our sister Viola Liuzzo who gave her life in the struggle for the right to vote... March 25, 1965." It names Evelyn G. Lowery as national convener and Joseph E. Lowery as SCLC president. Historical Marker Database puts it on U.S. 80 at milepost 111, 2.2 miles west of County Road 29, next to Wright Chapel A.M.E. Zion Church.

Liuzzo was born April 11, 1925, and in 1965 was a 39-year-old Detroit mother of five. She came to Selma after watching the March 7 attack on the Edmund Pettus Bridge and drove marchers for the SCLC. On the night of March 25, Klansmen shot her on Highway 80 while 19-year-old Leroy Moton was in the car. She is the only white woman honored on the Civil Rights Memorial in Montgomery. President Lyndon Johnson signed the Voting Rights Act on August 6, 1965. The Highway 80 monument has been vandalized.

paragraphs: The University of Alabama Department of Art and Art History says the Woods Quad Sculpture Garden grew for years and was officially dedicated in August 2014 by then-Dean Robert Olin. It sits among the quad's academic buildings and is part of a campus outdoor collection that began with the Alabama Biennial of the early 1990s.

Ringo Lisko's Flourish, on the east side of the quad's center, was unveiled in November 2021. It is the first sculpture in the McMahon-Pleiad Public Art Trail, a project of UA, UAB, and UAH funded by the UA System Board of Trustees. Lisko, a 2020 BFA major in sculpture and drawing, made an eight-foot cast-bronze crescent of camellias, the state flower: 93 blossoms on a stainless-steel frame.

Joe McCreary's Goldie 1971 (2009), iron and steel, about 23 feet long, 4 feet tall, and 5 feet wide, and between 3 and 4 tons, lies in front of Woods Hall at the northeast corner. It commemorates Sloss Furnaces and was purchased in 2010. Billy Lee's Homage to Brancusi, painted steel about 12 feet tall, won the 1993 Biennial purchase award and is the oldest sculpture still in the quad. Craig Wedderspoon's Riverstone and Quilted Vessel are also on the grounds.

paragraphs: In January 1958 the Catholic men's club in Silverton discussed a shrine to miners, hoping it might help an economy at its lowest ebb since the town began in 1874. The original plaque reads: "This shrine erected in honor of Christ of the Mines by the people of Silverton to ask God's blessing of the mining industry of the San Juans." A second plaque, added in 1982, commemorates lives spared when a lake above the Sunnyside mine flooded a portal on Sunday, June 4, 1978, while the mines were closed.

Deseret News says the shrine is above 10th and Bluff streets, reached by the dirt Shrine Road off Highway 550 north of town toward Ouray.
